I don’t think a Google review can fully capture what Kesha has been for me.

Back in September 2025, I had one of the worst anxiety attacks of my life. It was a Sunday, and I remember calling multiple therapists, but no one was available. In complete panic, I found Kesha’s number on Google and called her, barely able to speak through my tears, just saying I needed help.

What she did next is something I will never forget. Without hesitation, on a Sunday night, and despite not feeling well herself, she opened her clinic just to see me. She sat with me, calmed me down, and helped me get through that moment.

Over the following weeks and months, I continued to struggle with anxiety attacks, but she was always there. Whether it was picking up my calls, calming me over video calls, or guiding me through sessions, she showed up every single time with patience, warmth, and genuine care.

Therapy with her has never felt clinical or distant. It’s been safe, peaceful, and deeply comforting. She listens without judgment, understands without needing too many words, and helps you feel grounded even on your worst days.

I truly feel lucky to have found her when I did. For me, she wasn’t just a therapist in that moment, she was exactly the support I needed when everything felt overwhelming.

If you’re looking for someone who is not just professional but also incredibly compassionate and dependable, I cannot recommend Kesha enough. <3

Most men don’t talk about declining mental health.
They hide it behind work, anger, silence, scrolling, staying “busy,” or acting like everything is fine.

Sometimes the signs are not loud.
They quietly show up as:

• Constant overthinking
• Feeling emotionally numb
• Irritation over small things
• Losing interest in life
• Exhaustion that sleep doesn’t fix
• Escaping through distractions

Mental health awareness is not weakness.
And struggling silently does not make someone “less of a man.”

Healing starts when we stop pretending we’re okay all the time. 🤍

Overthinking is when your mind gets stuck in repetitive thoughts without reaching a useful conclusion. It often involves replaying past mistakes or worrying about future problems. Rather than solving anything, it’s usually a way to cope with anxiety or avoid uncomfortable emotions.

At its core, overthinking acts like a safety mechanism. The brain tries to stay in control by analyzing every detail. This creates a loop: a trigger leads to a negative thought, which causes stress, and that stress fuels even more thinking.

Common signs include mental exhaustion, feeling unable to “switch off,” and constant second-guessing. You may also notice physical symptoms like headaches, fatigue, or trouble sleeping. Overthinking often brings catastrophizing—imagining worst-case scenarios—and difficulty letting go of past events.

To manage it, start by noticing when you’re stuck in a thought loop without judging yourself. Then question the thought: is it based on facts, or just fear? Ask yourself if this thinking is helping or just draining your energy. Awareness is the first step to breaking the cycle.

Overthinking often feels like you’re being “careful” or “responsible,” but in reality, it slowly drains your energy and keeps you stuck in the same loop. The mind keeps replaying situations, creating worst-case scenarios, and making small decisions feel overwhelming. Over time, this habit can affect your confidence, sleep, and even your relationships.

What most people don’t realize is that overthinking is not a personality trait—it’s a learned mental pattern. And like any pattern, it can be changed with the right approach. The first step is awareness. Notice when your thoughts start looping. Instead of fighting them, pause and ask yourself: Is this helping me or just exhausting me? Shift your focus from “thinking more” to “taking one small action.”

Clarity doesn’t come from endless thinking—it comes from calmness and action.

Ask yourself today:
